title: Your First Mini-Project
story: You're making an 'About Me' card for a new friend. You want to introduce yourself, share your age, and show off a cool math trick. Instead of writing it on paper, you're going to write it in code — combining everything you've learned into one program that's uniquely yours.
why: Real programs aren't built from just one concept — they combine printing, variables, and math together. This is your first taste of how everything fits together to make something complete.
analogy: Programs are like Lego — you snap small pieces together (printing, variables, math) to build something bigger than any single piece could be on its own.
try_it: Add a variable for your favorite number. Print something about it — like what you get when you multiply it by 10. Can you also calculate and print how many days old you are (age × 365)?
tips: Build your program one piece at a time — write one line, test it, then add the next.
Use meaningful variable names: `birth_year` tells you exactly what's inside, while `x` doesn't.
Comments help you remember what each section does — think of them as section headers in a notebook.
You can do math with variables, not just plain numbers: `age + 5`, `current_year - age`, `hours * 60`.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to create a variable with `let` before using it — the variable must exist before you print or calculate with it.
Printing a variable with quotes: `io.println("age")` prints the word 'age', not the number stored inside.
Putting your `let` statements after your `io.println` calls — the computer reads top to bottom, so create your variables first.
Forgetting that changing a variable's value doesn't recalculate earlier lines — the computer reads your code once from top to bottom.
